grades.A: physics, or consistent RCT / meta-analysis support
grades.T: cultural tradition, not a scientific claim

claims.statement: Sound vibration makes visible standing-wave patterns on a water surface (Faraday waves, bowl modes, Chladni figures).
claims.plainSummary: Textbook physics since Faraday (1831) and Chladni (1787). Which exact pattern appears depends on the bowl, depth, temperature and drive level.
claims.whatWeSay: See your sound. Physics you can watch. Explore frequencies in real water.

claims.statement: Driving the water with two frequencies at certain ratios can produce 8-, 10- and 12-fold quasipatterns.
claims.plainSummary: Shown in controlled lab experiments, usually with viscous, shallow layers. Plain water in a bowl may not show them.
claims.whatWeSay: Experimental two-frequency mode: ordered patterns that never repeat, when conditions allow.

claims.statement: Cymatic patterns or sound-shaped water heal the body or 'structure' water.
claims.plainSummary: No good evidence. The patterns are a physical response of the surface; nothing persists in the water after the sound stops.
claims.whatWeSay: A beautiful physical effect of sound on water.

claims.statement: Binaural beats entrain brainwaves.
claims.plainSummary: Research is mixed; a 2023 systematic review of 14 EEG studies found results inconsistent.
claims.whatWeSay: An immersive headphone audio experience some people find relaxing.

claims.statement: Binaural beats reduce stress or pain.
claims.plainSummary: 2024 systematic reviews report mixed, low-certainty findings from small trials.
claims.whatWeSay: Some listeners describe the experience as calming.

claims.statement: Monaural and isochronic beats are audible on ordinary speakers; binaural beats need headphones.
claims.plainSummary: Binaural beats are created inside the listener from two different ear signals; monaural beats are a physical beat in the air.
claims.whatWeSay: Room-speaker beats work for groups; binaural layers need headphones.

claims.statement: Bilateral or hemispheric audio synchronises the two brain hemispheres.
claims.plainSummary: No good evidence for 'hemisphere synchronisation'. We offer these as experiential audio modes only.
claims.whatWeSay: Experiential audio modes: sound that moves between your ears.

claims.statement: These nine tones (174-963 Hz) are popular 'solfeggio' tradition frequencies.
claims.plainSummary: A modern invention (1970s, Joseph Puleo, later popularised). Offered as a cultural/musical choice.
claims.whatWeSay: Popular tradition frequencies.

claims.statement: Solfeggio frequencies repair DNA, remove toxins or have other specific effects.
claims.plainSummary: No scientific evidence for specific effects.
claims.whatWeSay: (nothing - we attach no benefits to these tones)

claims.statement: Tuning to A4 = 432 Hz has special or natural effects.
claims.plainSummary: No established evidence that 432 Hz tuning has special effects.
claims.whatWeSay: Selectable reference pitch (440 Hz default, 432 Hz available).
claims.notes: Spec 17 lists no source on 432 Hz; add one before using this in a Learn card.

claims.statement: The Schumann resonance (~7.83 Hz) is a natural electromagnetic resonance of the Earth-ionosphere cavity.
claims.plainSummary: Real atmospheric physics, measured since the 1960s.
claims.whatWeSay: A natural electromagnetic resonance of the Earth; no established health link.
claims.notes: Spec 17 lists no source for this entry; add one (e.g. a geophysics review) before using it in Learn.

claims.statement: Listening to or being exposed to 7.83 Hz improves health.
claims.plainSummary: No established health link.
claims.whatWeSay: (nothing)

claims.statement: Resonance breathing near 0.1 Hz (about 4.5-6.5 breaths/min) increases heart-rate variability, and HRV biofeedback can help some people relax.
claims.plainSummary: Supported by multiple trials and reviews of HRV biofeedback (Lehrer & Gevirtz).
claims.whatWeSay: A breathing pacer at about six breaths a minute.

claims.statement: Heart-rhythm coherence improves emotions, intuition or performance broadly.
claims.plainSummary: Mostly observational or industry-linked studies; broader claims go beyond the evidence.
claims.whatWeSay: A heart-rhythm coherence readout (not a medical measurement).
claims.notes: 'HeartMath-style method' wording is allowed in Learn cards and docs only, never in marketing.

claims.statement: Five minutes a day of cyclic sighing for a month improved mood and lowered breathing rate more than mindfulness meditation in one randomized trial.
claims.plainSummary: A single RCT (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine 2023). Promising, not settled.
claims.whatWeSay: A guided cyclic-sigh breathing exercise.

claims.statement: A 7-day meditation retreat produced measurable brain and blood changes.
claims.plainSummary: One observational study of 20 healthy adults with no control group; the program's founder was a co-author employed by the retreat company; critics point to confounds.
claims.whatWeSay: Guided phases inspired by meditation practice, described generically.

claims.statement: Mindfulness, the relaxation response and yoga nidra reduce stress.
claims.plainSummary: NOT YET GRADED. The spec requires looking up a current meta-analysis before assigning a grade.
claims.whatWeSay: (not used until graded)

claims.statement: Flashing or flickering light at about 3-30 Hz (up to 60 Hz for some people) can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.
claims.plainSummary: Well-established; the reason the Safety Guardian blocks 3-60 Hz flicker and there is no strobe mode.
claims.whatWeSay: This experience uses light. If you have epilepsy or light sensitivity, check with your clinician first.

claims.statement: Watching moving water and light is a calm, pleasant focal point for many people.
claims.plainSummary: Describes the experience, not a health effect. Testimonials must stay about the experience ('beautiful', 'the room went quiet'), never health outcomes.
claims.whatWeSay: A calm, beautiful focal point for meditation. An immersive group sound experience.

claims.statement: Transposing a tone up by octaves into light frequencies gives its 'colour'.
claims.plainSummary: Sound and light are different physical waves; the octave-colour map is an artistic metaphor, not a physical equivalence.
claims.whatWeSay: Octave colour: an artistic metaphor, not a physical equivalence.

claims.statement: Simulated patterns and predicted wavelengths come from linear wave models (dispersion relation, bowl modes, N-wave sums).
claims.plainSummary: The models are standard physics, but real bowls differ; simulations are labelled SIMULATION and predictions as Simulated or Estimated.
claims.whatWeSay: Predicted from physics; your bowl's calibration shows the real thing.
